faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Chestertown?
faqs.a: Chestertown's historic core sets its own pricing logic. A bat exclusion on a brick colonial near the river involves a tall, complex roofline and sealing fitted to old mortar and trim — more craft than a suburban gable vent, and priced that way after inspection. A mid-century home on the outer streets with squirrels at the eaves is a standard job, and a farm-edge property adds groundhog burrows and outbuildings. We inspect the specific building, explain what its age and construction require, and give the complete figure before removal or sealing work begins.

faqs.q: Bats are roosting in a historic Chestertown attic — how is that handled without harming the house?
faqs.a: Slowly and precisely. The inspection maps every entry — on 200-year-old Chestertown rooflines the gaps are usually settled joints, chimney flashing, and louvered vents rather than chewed holes. Maryland bat work is non-lethal exclusion only: one-way exits on the active entries, the remaining gaps sealed with materials fitted to the historic fabric and removable without damage, timed to the DNR-recommended September 1 to March 1 window, with prior state approval required for larger colonies during the spring and summer pup season. The colony leaves on its own wings; the house keeps its character and loses its tenants.

Chestertown.wildlife_intro:
Chestertown is Kent County's seat and one of Maryland's best-preserved colonial river ports, set on the Chester River with a historic district of brick 1700s and 1800s homes, Washington College, and a working waterfront. The river and the college define the calls: bats in the tall historic attics and the college-area rooflines, raccoons in the chimneys of the brick colonials, and rats around the waterfront and food businesses along the river blocks.

The neighborhoods step from the historic core into mid-century streets and then into farmland within a mile in most directions, adding groundhogs under outbuildings, skunks under porches, and opossums everywhere. The Chester River's marshy tributaries keep raccoon numbers high, and the town's mature canopy keeps squirrels in the attics of the older streets each fall. Like Annapolis, Chestertown work is historic-fabric work: fitted caps and screens, mortar-aware sealing, and exclusion that respects buildings older than the republic. The Delmarva fox squirrel lives in the mature woods around the county — protected and uncommon, a sighting to enjoy and a referral if one ever conflicts with a building, never a routine removal.

faqs.q: Our Rock Hall cottage sat empty all winter and animals moved in — what now?
faqs.a: That is the most common Rock Hall call, and the order of operations matters. First we identify what wintered in the house — squirrels in the attic, a raccoon in the crawlspace, or bats in the peak each need different handling — and remove the animals present. Then the cleanup is assessed, because a winter of droppings in insulation is a health matter, not just a smell. Finally the house is sealed properly: chimney capped, vents screened with anchored mesh, crawlspace secured. Going forward, a closing inspection each fall and an opening check each spring is the routine that keeps a seasonal cottage from becoming a seasonal den.

faqs.q: Raccoons raid the marinas near my Rock Hall home — can anything be done?
faqs.a: The raccoons themselves are responding to crab and fish waste around the harbor, and no removal program at your house changes the harbor. What changes your situation is whether they can den and shelter at your address. We remove raccoons living in a cottage, boathouse, or crawlspace and seal those structures thoroughly, and we will advise on the food side — secured trash, no scraps left out, pet food indoors. Maryland prohibits relocating raccoons, so the durable answer is a sealed building on a street where the easy dens disappear one by one. Harbor raccoons remain; harbor raccoons in your attic do not have to.

Rock Hall.wildlife_intro:
Rock Hall is a watermen's town on the Chesapeake Bay at Kent County's western edge — marinas, seafood houses, and a grid of cottages and modest homes a short walk from the harbor in any direction. The bay runs the wildlife program here: raccoons work the marinas, crab scraps, and trash, and den in the crawlspaces and attics of the cottages; rats hold on around the harbor businesses where food waste is a way of life.

Seasonal homes are Rock Hall's multiplier, just as in every bay town: cottages empty through the winter host squirrels and raccoons undisturbed, and the spring opening reveals the damage all at once. Skunks and opossums den under the raised cottages, bats summer in the older rooflines and boathouses, and groundhogs keep to the open ground at the town's farm edges. The marshes around the town hold muskrat and abundant bird life as background, and the occasional Delmarva fox squirrel appears in the mature stands inland — protected, and left alone. The Rock Hall prescription is seasonal discipline: a thorough exclusion before the winter closing, a check before the spring opening, and caps and screens that survive both the weather and the raccoons.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Galena?
faqs.a: Galena work is priced the way the properties present: plainly. A chimney raccoon in an in-town home is one figure; adding the groundhog system under the barn and the skunk den at the porch makes it a property program, still usually completed in a small number of visits because everything is at ground level and accessible. Farm properties with several outbuildings take longer to inspect than to treat. We walk the house and the structures with you, price each piece, and give the total before trapping or sealing starts — and we will tell you if a piece, like a snake that is best left in the barn, should not be billed at all.

faqs.q: What keeps getting into Galena crawlspaces?
faqs.a: Skunks and opossums, entering through the broken or missing vent covers that older Galena homes accumulate over the decades, with raccoons using any opening large enough to squeeze a shoulder through. The drainages behind the farm-edge streets deliver a steady supply of all three. We check who is actually residing before any screening — a mother skunk with young in May changes the timing — remove the animals, and replace the vent covers with anchored, framed screening that a raccoon cannot peel. Replacing like with like, a screen for a screen, fails within a season here; the framing is the fix.

Galena.wildlife_intro:
Galena is a small crossroads town in northeastern Kent County, near the Sassafras River country and the Delaware line, where a compact grid of older homes sits inside a sea of farmland. It is quiet, agricultural Maryland, and its wildlife calls are the farm-town set in pure form.

Groundhogs lead: burrow systems along the field edges, under the barns and sheds, and beneath the porches of the in-town homes nearest the fields. Raccoons den in the chimneys of the older houses and commute from the creek bottoms; skunks work the lawns and den under outbuildings; bats take the tall attics of the Victorian-era homes in summer. Black rat snakes are part of the working landscape around grain storage, protected and generally tolerated once identified. The Sassafras watershed's wooded bottoms west of town keep a steady flow of opossums and raccoons along the drainages behind the properties. Galena jobs are usually blessedly legible — the burrow is visible, the chimney is uncapped, the crawlspace vent is broken — and the value of the visit is doing all of it in one pass, so the property stops rotating animals through the same three openings year after year.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Millington attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night-only scratching in Kent County often means bats, flying squirrels or raccoons, while daytime running usually points to gray squirrels. Around Chester River, the cover close to housing means several species are plausible, so call us for an inspection and we will identify the animal before anything is sealed.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Millington porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Millington with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

Millington.wildlife_intro:
Millington gives our crew a Kent mix shaped by Chester River and the housing around it. Raccoons and bats in Chestertown's colonial-era homes and Rock Hall's waterfront houses lead Kent County's calls, groundhogs work the farm edges around Galena and Kennedyville, and skunks den under the county's many porches and sheds — and Millington is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Chestertown is a colonial port town of brick Federal homes, Rock Hall is a watermen's town, Galena and Millington are small farm villages, and the rest is farmhouses and waterfront estates. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Millington; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Millington jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.
